paper_title: Rethinking Relative Policy Differences Transfer of On-Policy Distillation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a target policy on its own rollouts using token-level supervision from a stronger teacher, but typically relies on the teacher being substantially more capable than the target. Recent work relaxes this requirement by transferring the relative policy difference between an expert and a reference policy rather than the expert's absolute distribution. Yet it remains unclear which differences provide useful supervision and which targets can benefit from them. We develop a unified view in which the log-probability ratio between a proxy expert and a proxy reference defines an implicit reward for KL-regularized policy optimization. This formulation induces an on-policy update for the target, recovers conventional OPD as a special case, and enables any-to-any transfer across models that differ in scale, training stage or generation. Our systematic experiments yield three findings. First, a stronger expert is not necessarily a better source of supervision: differences induced by task-specific training, including reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning, transfer consistently, whereas those arising from model scale alone transfer weakly or not at all. Second, the expert and reference serve complementary roles: the expert provides the capability to be transferred, while the reference filters out shared behavior and isolates the relevant residual. Third, even a useful difference does not transfer to every target: success requires the induced update to move the target toward the expert and generalize beyond sampled rollouts. Raw policy distance does not predict transferability, whereas an appropriate reference can rescue otherwise unsuccessful transfer. These results characterize when relative policy differences provide effective supervision for OPD.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as an important approach to post-training large language models (LLM) [1, 2, 3, 4]. By eliciting teacher guidance on samples generated by the student itself, OPD mitigates the distribution shift between offline data and the student policy while providing more targeted training signals. However, conventional OPD directly encourages the student policy to approximate the teacher policy, making its effectiveness dependent on the teachers performance advantage over the student. When the two models have comparable capabilities, or when the teacher is weaker, distillation often yields limited gains and may even impair the students existing capabilities. Consequently, OPD typically requires substantially stronger teacher [5, 6], restricting its applicability and limiting the reuse of existing post-training outcomes. To reduce this dependence on the teachers absolute capability, recent studies have explored relative policy update transfer [7, 8, 9]. Rather than directly aligning the output distributions of student and teacher, this approach extracts the relative policy update induced by post-training by comparing the teacher model before and after training, 1 and then transfers this update to the proxy target model. It therefore does not require the teacher to substantially outperform the student; it only requires the post-trained teacher to outperform its corresponding base model. By shifting the transfer target from the teachers output distribution to the policy change induced by its post-training, this paradigm broadens the applicability of OPD across models of different scales and architectures, and offers promising way to reuse costly post-training outcomes. Despite its promise, the scope of relative policy update transfer remains poorly understood. Existing studies typically consider narrow class of source pairs, in which the expert is obtained by applying reinforcement learning (RL) [10] to the reference model. It is therefore unclear whether policy differences arising from other sources, such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) [11, 12] or model scaling [13, 14], provide equally useful supervision. Moreover, prior work has largely focused on demonstrating transfer gains, with limited analysis of how the expert, reference and target jointly determine the outcome. As result, the conditions under which policy difference is useful and transferable remain unclear. In this work, we revisit relative policy difference transfer through the lens of implicit reward and formally derive its transfer objective. The derivation interprets the policy difference between proxy expert and proxy reference model as the supervision transferred to target model, while clarifying the distinct roles of all three models. It further separates two questions that are often conflated: whether source pair encodes useful improvement [15], and whether given target can realize that improvement. Guided by this derivation, we conduct systematic empirical study across policy differences induced by RL, SFT and model scaling, as well as across target models with different initial policies. Specifically, we ask: (i) Which policy differences provide useful supervision? (ii) Which capabilities of the expert are transferred, and what role does the reference play? (iii) Which target models can effectively realize useful policy difference? Our results reveal three main findings. (i) stronger model is not necessarily better source of supervision. Improvements acquired through task-directed training transfer consistently, whether induced by RL or SFT, whereas differences caused by model scaling alone transfer weakly or unreliably. (ii) the proxy expert and proxy reference play distinct and complementary roles: the expert provides the capability, while the reference filters out behaviors already shared by the two models, exposing the remaining improvement for transfer [16]. (iii) useful policy difference is not universally transferable. Transfer succeeds when the induced update moves the target toward the expert and generalizes beyond the training samples. Raw policy distance does not predict this compatibility; critically, an appropriate reference can recover an otherwise failed transfer. Our contributions are: We formally derive relative policy difference transfer from implicit rewards and formulate an any-to-any OPD objective that distinguishes the roles of the proxy expert, reference, and target. We systematically evaluate policy differences induced by RL, SFT, and model scaling across diverse targets, showing how the expert, reference, and target jointly shape transfer outcomes. We characterize when policy differences are useful and transferable, identifying task-directed training, reference filtering, and target compatibility as the key factors governing transfer.

sections.title: 2.1 On-Policy Distillation
sections.content: On-policy distillation (OPD) combines on-policy sampling with dense supervision: the student generates trajectories, and the teacher scores each token on student-visited states [1, 2]. OPD typically minimizes the reverse KL, which is mode-seeking and avoids forcing lower-capacity student to model the teachers long tail [17]. Its gradient is equivalent to policy-gradient update with dense token-level reward rt = log πT (at st) log πθ(at st), or, equivalently, KL-constrained RL with teacher reward log πT (at st) and unit KL weight [18, 19]. This dense, on-policy supervision improves sample efficiency, reduces distribution shift by training on states visited by the student, and mitigates catastrophic forgetting associated with off-policy SFT [3, 1, 20]. Related self-distillation methods similarly acquire new skills while preserving prior capabilities without explicit rewards [21, 22]. OPD has therefore become common component of production post-training pipelines. Qwen3 [3] first uses off-policy distillation to establish reasoning capabilities and then OPD for logit alignment. MiMo-V2-Flash further scales this approach through multiple domain-specialized RL teachers, enabling 309B/15B-active student to match models with 23 more total parameters [23]. However, OPD relies on sufficiently stronger teacher: because its reward is derived from teacher log-probabilities on student trajectories, the signal becomes uninformative when teacher and student policies are too similar [24].

sections.title: 2.2 Relative Policy Differences in Post-Training
sections.content: As mentioned above, OPD remains informative only when the teacher is sufficiently stronger than the student, since it directly uses the teachers log-probability as reward [24, 25]. Recent work relaxes this requirement by transferring how teacher improves rather than its final policy. Given reference policy πref and its adapted expert πexp, these methods use the log-ratio log πexp(a s) log πref (a s) on student rollouts as dense learning signal. The student thus follows direction of improvement instead of matching an absolute distribution. Existing methods construct the referenceexpert pair through instruction tuning [7], reinforcement learning on weaker model [8], or reward-based optimization of an auxiliary proxy policy [9]. Because only the policy difference is transferred, the source model need not outperform the student, allowing weaker, older, or independently trained models to provide useful supervision. Despite promising results across domains, prior work provides limited understanding of when and across which models relative policy transfer succeeds. Its effectiveness depends on both how the referenceexpert pair is constructed and which target model receives the resulting policy shift. Existing studies largely evaluate specific pairs on students from the same model generation and at similar scales. It remains unclear which relative policies are useful, whether they transfer across models with different priors or capability levels, and when their benefits vanish. We systematically vary both the source policy pair and the target model to characterize effective relative policies and the boundaries of their transferability.

sections.title: 3.2 From Absolute to Relative Matching: An Implicit Reward Perspective
sections.content: A key feature of conventional OPD is that the same reference policy appears in both the reward-like term and the KL regularizer. These two occurrences of πref cancel, reducing the objective to direct matching of the teacher distribution. This coupling makes conventional OPD an absolute matching method, which can be restrictive when the teacher and target have poorly aligned output distributions [24]. Thus, ϕ preserves the action-wise reward differences induced by r, up to the positive scale 1/τ , and provides an implicit reward parameterization through the proxy policy difference [26]. We formalize this relative matching procedure in the next subsection.

sections.title: 4.1 Experiment Setup and Metrics
sections.content: Protocol. All experiments optimize the same objective (Eq. 11) with fixed transfer strength α/β = 1. Models are drawn from the Qwen3 and Qwen2.5 families. For efficiency, all experiments use the top-16 token distribution instead of the full vocabulary [24]. Training and evaluation. We follow the prior work [9], proxy pairs are obtained by RL or SFT on DeepMath103K [27] for math and Eurus-RL-Code [28] for code, using ruled verifiable reward. Sampling uses temperature 1.0 and top-p 1.0 for both training and evaluation. We evaluate on eight math benchmarks (AIME24/25/26, SMT25, CMIMC25, HMMT25-Feb/Nov, HMMT26-Feb) with 16 samples, and on three code benchmarks (HumanEval+, MBPP+, LCB) with 8 samples. Model details are in Appendix B. Metrics. Let (π) denote the average task performance of policy π. We measure the proxy pair capability gain and the target model improvement as GP = (π+ ϕ ) (πϕ), GT = (π θ ) (πref ), (12) and report Rperf = GT /GP to compare their scales. These metrics describe the policy difference and its transfer in performance space. We further use KLd diagnostics to characterize transfer beyond performance differences. KProxy quantifies the proxy expertreference difference, and KBase the proxytarget reference gap. KTarget quantifies the difference between the target reference and the optimized target. KInduced quantifies the difference between KTarget and the distribution induced by the proxy log-policy difference. sections.title: 4.2 Which Policy Differences Provide Useful Supervision?
sections.content: A stronger proxy expert may differ from its reference for two main reasons: task-specific optimization, or simply larger scale. We ask whether these two sources of difference provide equally useful supervision. We fix Qwen3-8B as the target and compare nine proxy pairs constructed from RL and SFT updates, scale gaps, and one alternative reference. Task-directed optimization creates transferable differences. Eq. 4 shows that KL-regularized task optimization makes log π+ ϕ log πϕ encode task-relevant update. More broadly, this interpretation applies approximately to experts obtained through rewardd RL or SFT with offline data, even without explicit KL regularization. In contrast, scale differences between independently trained models need not encode task-relevant direction. Table 2 follows this split. All task-optimized differences improve the target: the RL and SFT pairs yield GT ranging from 9.78 to 32.23, and Qwen3-4B-RL with an alternative Qwen3-1.7B reference achieves 25.85, showing that the reference need not be experts training origin. In contrast, the four scale-only pairs yield much smaller target gains, despite positive proxy pair capability gaps. sections.title: Takeaway
sections.content: A stronger model is not automatically better teacher. Improvements from optimizing toward an explicit or implicit task reward, whether by RL or SFT, transfer consistently, while improvements from increasing model size alone transfer weakly or unreliably.

sections.title:
4.3 Which Part of the Expert’s Capability Gets Transferred?
A policy difference is jointly defined by proxy expert and proxy reference. Section 4.2 showed that the difference
must encode a task-optimized capability; here we ask how the expert and reference each shape that capability. We
fix Qwen3-8B as the target, and study two controlled sweeps: fixing the reference to Qwen3-4B while varying the
expert, and fixing the expert to Qwen3-4B-RL while varying the reference.
The expert sets how much capability is available. With the reference fixed to Qwen3-4B, moving the expert
from the early to the regular and late RL checkpoints raises GP from 22.09 to 26.89 and 32.28, and GT tracks this
trend (22.42 → 26.84 → 28.18; Table 3). A stronger expert thus makes more capability available, although the
additional capability is only partly realized as the expert grows stronger (Rperf falls from 1.015 to 0.873).
The reference isolates the residual capability for transfer. Fixing the expert to Qwen3-4B-RL and changing the
reference shows the complementary role. Replacing Qwen3-4B with the early RL checkpoint cuts GT from 26.84
to 9.62, because the difference now exposes only the increment from the early to the regular checkpoint, rather than
the full increment over the base. The reference therefore acts as a filter: it removes the capability already shared
with the expert and leaves only the residual for transfer. This filter need not be the expert’s training origin. Using
Qwen2.5-3B as the reference gives the largest target gain (29.09), despite the largest KBase = 1.23.
Token-level overlap reveals the residual selected by the reference. To directly examine the filtering effect, we
measure the top-16 overlap ratio OE,R between the proxy expert and proxy reference on the same fixed set of target
states. With Qwen3-4B-RL fixed as the expert, OE,R decreases from 0.916 with the early-RL reference to 0.839
with Qwen3-4B and 0.625 with Qwen2.5-3B. The corresponding target gains increase from 9.62 to 26.84 and 29.09.
sections.content: 7 Figure 3: Effects of the proxy expert and reference on transfer. Qwen3-8B is fixed as the target. Thus, reference that shares more high-probability tokens with expert removes more of the experts policy change, leaving smaller residual for transfer. This pattern is not merely restatement of the association between GP and GT observed in Section 4.2. The early-to-regular and regular-to-late RL increments have similar proxy gains (GP = 4.80 and 5.39), but different expertreference overlaps (0.916 and 0.869), and produce much larger target gain (25.03 vs. 9.62). Therefore, similar target performance gains can encode substantially different policy-space residuals. The reference determines not only how much proxy performance differs, but also the structure and strength of the update presented to the target.

sections.title: Takeaway
sections.content: The expert supplies the capability, while the reference filters out what the two models already share, leaving the remaining difference for transfer.

Applying one difference to different targets gives sharply different outcomes. Qwen3 targets gain ranging from 9.78 to 29.09, whereas Qwen2.5 targets under Qwen3 reference gain almost nothing (GT [2.46, 2.72]). Whether difference helps is thus property of the target, not of the difference alone. natural assumption is that target benefits when it is close to the proxy pair, but Figure 4 rejects this: neither Rperf nor transferred accuracy is monotone in the KBase, and Qwen3 targets gain even at the largest KBase (Rperf 0.65 at KBase > 1.2). The outcome splits by model family, not by distance. 8 Figure 4: The outcome is not function of policy distance. Performance realization ratio (left) and transferred math accuracy (right) against the proxytarget base KL. (a) Overlap with the proxy expert (b) Overlap with expert vs. target base Figure 5: Benefiting targets move toward the proxy expert(fixed Qwen3-1.7B proxy pair). Generation compatibility, not the difference, controls the outcome. To test whether the family split is causal, we hold the difference fixed and change only the references family. Replacing the Qwen3 reference with Qwen2.5 one (the Qwen3-4B-RL / Qwen2.5-3B pair) turns the Qwen2.5 targets from near-zero or negative gains into positive ones (GT = 6.74/2.25/5.76), while Qwen3 targets stay successful  (Table 4)  . This intervention shows that transfer failure is not an intrinsic limitation of the target or the useful difference. Instead, the reference determines whether the difference is presented in form that the target can learn and generalize from; matching the model family is one effective choice in our experiments. Benefiting means moving toward the expert and generalizing. Two diagnostics explain what compatibility buys. First, benefiting targets move toward the expert: for fixed Qwen3-1.7B proxy pair, the Qwen3 targets overlap with the proxy expert rises steadily while the Qwen2.5 targets stay flat (Figure 5a); tracking both references confirms the direction, as the benefiting target (GT = +16.1) moves toward the expert and away from its own base, whereas the failing target (GT = 1.7) moves toward neither (Figure 5b). Second, this movement must generalize: for the incompatible Qwen2.5-Math-7B target, training accuracy rises and even spikes but validation accuracy stays near zero, so the update fits the training problems without transferring (Figure 6a). Matching the reference generation restores both: overlap with the expert grows and validation accuracy rises, while cross-generation references make both collapse (Figure 6b). Failure is therefore not undertraining but an inability to move toward the expert in way that generalizes.

sections.title: Takeaway
sections.content: A useful policy difference is not automatically transferable to every target. Transfer succeeds when the induced update moves the target toward the proxy expert and generalizes beyond the training examples. Raw policy distance does not predict this behavior, while choosing an appropriate reference can recover an otherwise failed transfer. 9 (a) Train vs. validation across targets (b) Effect of the reference family Figure 6: Failure is not undertraining, and matching the reference generation recovers the benefit.

sections.title: 4.5 Do the Transfer Patterns Generalize across Domains?
sections.content: The preceding findings are established on mathematical reasoning tasks. We next examine whether the same qualitative transfer patterns appear in code generation. We select representative successful and failed configurations and evaluate matched configurations on both math and code. For each setting, we report the target gain GT over the corresponding target base in Table 5. Table 5: Representative successful and failed settings performance on both math and code. Transfer between Qwen3 models is positive on both math (+26.8 and +25.9) and code (+2.3 and +1.9). By contrast, transferring Qwen3-derived difference to Qwen2.5 target fails in both domains, producing gains of 1.7 and 6.4, respectively. Settings with an uninformative also yield no useful target improvement in either domain. Finally, the Qwen2.5-based proxy pair transfers successfully to Qwen3-8B on both math (+24.6) and code (+9.1), showing that the cross-domain consistency is not restricted to same-generation transfer. Although the gains are generally smaller on code, the signs and relative ordering of the tested configurations remain consistent across the two domains.

sections.title: Takeaway
sections.content: Transfer patterns persist across tasks: configurations that succeed or fail on math show the same qualitative outcomes on code.

sections.title:
5 Conclusion
In this work, we revisited relative policy difference transfer through the lens of implicit reward. This perspective
leads to A2-OPD, an any-to-any formulation that decouples the proxy pair defining the relative difference from the
target receiving it, with conventional OPD recovered as a special case. Our experiments further characterize the
opportunities and limits of this generality. Policy differences induced by task-directed training, including RL and
SFT, transfer consistently, whereas differences due to model scaling alone are often ineffective. We also find that the
proxy expert supplies the capability to be transferred, while the proxy reference determines the residual presented to
the target. Finally, transfer depends on target compatibility: a useful difference must induce an update that the target
can follow and generalize from, and an appropriate reference can recover some otherwise unsuccessful transfers.
Together, these results clarify when any-to-any relative policy difference transfer provides effective supervision and
offer practical guidance for selecting proxy pairs and targets.

sections.title: B Experimental and Implementation Details
sections.content: Models. For math, the regular RL expert is trained for 500 steps, while the early and late experts are taken at 100 and 1,200 steps, respectively. For code, the RL expert is trained for 300 steps. Qwen3-4BSFT denotes Qwen3-4B fine-tuned on correct trajectories rejection-sampled from DeepMath-103K using Skywork-7B: 14,716 of the 15,491 trajectories are used for training and 775 for validation. SFT is configured for three epochs (229 steps) and stops at step 70 under early stopping with patience of 5. 14 Training Details. Our implementation follows the on-policy training setup of P-OPD. For each prompt, the target policy samples eight responses with temperature 1.0 and top-p 1.0. We use training batch size of 1024, learning rate of 1 106, and maximum response length of 16,384 tokens. The proxy expert, proxy reference, and target reference remain frozen, and gradients are applied only to the target policy. For models with different tokenizers, we use text as an intermediate representation to map target tokens into the proxy token space and retain only successfully aligned tokens for training. We train for 80 steps in the math domain and 150 steps in the code domain. In both domains, the gradient norm has reached stable plateau by the end of training. Math experiments use DeepMath-103K, while code experiments use Eurus-RL-Code. Unless otherwise stated, math results are reported as Mean@16 and code results as Mean@8. Metrics.
